edits.english: MISHNA: Rabbi Yishmael says: Three days before them, meaning before the festivals of the gentiles, and three days after them, it is prohibited to engage in business with the gentiles. And the Rabbis say: Before their festivals it is prohibited, but after their festivals it is permitted.

The Jerusalem Talmud records a dispute regarding the reasoning of Rabbi Yishmael. Some explain that his ruling is based on the fact that gentiles are accustomed to adding days to their festival, similar to the Jewish custom of observing the day after a Festival as Isru Ĥag; therefore, the days following their festival are considered like the festival day itself. Rabbi Abba explains that the reasoning is that if a gentile knows that a Jew will not conduct business with him on the day following the festival, he will diminish his celebration of idol worship in order to save resources for the next day. The early commentaries explained the ruling according to the reasoning that the gentile “goes and gives thanks,” meaning that because of the proximity to the day of his idol’s festival, he goes and gives thanks on the following days as well. Alternatively, the prohibition against conducting business during the three days after the festival is a rabbinic decree due to the prohibition that applies during the three days before the festival (see Ra’ah and Meiri).
